title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of training-data provenance: Suno ingested copyrighted recordings at scale, reportedly including content scraped from YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, without securing licenses from rights holders. The consequence surfaced at inference time, when the deployed system could reproduce recognisable portions of protected songs in response to simple descriptive prompts. That is a downstream output failure with a traceable upstream cause, the composition of the training set, and it is the kind of failure that a rights-clearance review before training would have been positioned to catch.

The outputs themselves are the core evidentiary problem. Record labels showed that prompts describing an artist's era, genre, and name reliably produced audio closely mimicking specific copyrighted tracks. This is not a case of a model hallucinating a false fact but of a generative system reproducing stylistic and melodic content close enough to originals that the similarity is audible and demonstrable. No technical safeguard at the output stage, such as a similarity filter against a catalogue of protected works, appears to have been in place.

What is not established is intent. Allegations of deliberate concealment of training data sources are claims made in litigation, and a lawsuit is not a verdict. A German court found against Suno in the GEMA case, and some label lawsuits reached settlements, but the broader US litigation and class actions remain unresolved, and no court has yet issued a final finding on all claims.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping copyrighted music without permission and directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their generated outputs. The record labels claim the companies have been deliberately hiding what music they used to train their models, though both previously claimed this constitutes fair use. The lawsuits include a massive list of thousands of copyrighted works allegedly scraped for training, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly generate AI songs that closely replicate famous copyrighted tracks by using specific prompts describing the song's era, genre, and artist. For example, prompting for "1954 rock and roll billy haley comets" produced outputs mimicking Bill Haley's style, and a prompt for Mariah Carey produced a near-identical clone of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits, filed in New York and Massachusetts, include a thumb drive of problematic AI-generated music as evidence and represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services can be trained.
